Order:

(per the Hon'ble Sri Justice P.SAM KOSHY) Heard Mr. Umesh Singh learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. Swaroop Oorilla, learned Special Government Pleader appearing on behalf of the Additional Advocate-General for the respondents.

2. The instant is a writ petition which has been filed challenging the order dated 03.01.2022 (Annexure P-1) passed by respondent No.2 putting detenu under preventive detention under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the "The Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers,
Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders,
Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders,
Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (for short, 'the Act of 1986').
3. The writ petition is one which has been filed seeking for issuance of a Writ in the nature of Habeas Corpus with prayer for production of the detenu before the Court and quashment of the aforementioned orders.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 4. The facts of the case in brief are that the detenu has committed an offence under Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986 across various Police Station limits where detenu was involved in NDPS Act engaged in illegal and highly dangerous activities of peddling Contraband Cannabis / Ganja among the innocents which was registered within the jurisdiction of Hyderabad and Cyberabad Police Commissionerate indicating a pattern of persistent and organized drug trafficking.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: On 25.10.2021, the police authorities had apprehended the detenu near St. Anns College Lane, Mehdipatnam, in connection with the possession and peddling of 'Ganja' (marijuana), a narcotic substance prohibited under NDPS Act.
Upon arrest, the police authorities seized 1120 grams of Ganja packed in 28 covers of 40 grams each, a Jio cell phone, a Honda Destini scooter without number plate and Rs.2,000/- in cash.

The seizure was conducted under a confession-cum-seizure panchanama and samples were sent to the Telangana State Forensic Science Laboratories (TSFSL) in Red Hills, Hyderabad, which confirmed the substance as 'Ganja'.

The detenu was charged under Case No.243/2021, Section 8(c) read with Section 20(b) of the NDPS Act,
and was subsequently remanded to judicial custody.

entities.text: Case No.243/2021, Section 8(c) read with Section 20(b)
entities.label: CASE_NUMBER

sentences.text:
Previously, the detenu was arrested in four Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/
1 cases related to Ganja peddling offenses in Hyderabad and one in Cyberabad establishing a pattern of habitual drug related activities.

sentences.text: Despite being granted conditional bail in previous cases, the authority concerned believed that he is likely continue his illegal activities.

The authority concerned expressed grave concern over the impact of detenu's actions involved in procuring Ganja from undisclosed sources and selling it to the innocent people especially youth; for easy money, posing significant threat to society and also causing irreparable damages to their central nervous system and thereby crippling the mental and physical health of the people.

Due to the severity and repetitive nature of the offence, the authority concerned passed the preventive detention order on 03.01.2022 and classified detenu as "Drug-Offender".
5.

Thus, the impugned order was under challenged on the grounds that these alleged crimes fall under the purview of ordinary law and do not constitute a disturbance of public order, questioning the necessity and legality of the detention order under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act.

entities.text: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 6. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that a plain reading of the impugned order would reveal that the detention order against the detenu is unconstitutional and illegal.

He argued that the detention order does not warrant invocation of preventive detention laws and that the detaining authority failed to differentiate between acts affecting law and order and those affecting public order.

Further, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the authority concerned did not consider the detenu's compliance with bail conditions and his lack of involvement in other cases since release.
Furthermore, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended that detention order has passed mechanically without proper application of mind and based on flimsy grounds.

7. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that there is insufficient material to justify treating the detenu as a drug offender under the Act of 1986 and that the cases mentioned can be dealt with under ordinary law.

Additionally, the detaining authority allegedly failed to consider the conditional bail granted in four cases, which already placed the detenu under police surveillance making preventive detention unnecessary.
Further, it was argued that there is lack of prima facie evidence against the detenu in the registered cases and the complaints are vague and also intended to harass him.
Moreover, respondent No.2 did not follow the mandatory procedure before invoking the provisions of Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the Act of 1986 rendering the detention order liable to set aside.

8. Per contra, the learned Special Government Pleader argued that the detenu is a habitual drug offender and his involvement in multiple cases of Ganja peddling within the Hyderabad Police Commissionerate and one in Cyberabad.

Moreover, there are multiple cases registered against the detenu including Cr.No.11 of 2021 at Shahinayathgunj Police Station, Cr.No.18 of 2021 at Shahinayathgunj Police Station, Cr.No.124 of 2021 at Prohibition and Excise Station, Dhoolpet,
Cr.No.243 of 2021 of Asifnagar Police Station and Cr.No.849 of 2018 at Mailardevpally Police Station, Cyberabad.

All these cases clearly demonstrate that the detenu's ongoing engagement in drug trafficking, despite previous arrest and legal action, the detenu continued his engagement in illegal activities, particularly the peddling of Ganja which shows a pattern of behavior that poses an ongoing threat to public order and health.

Furthermore, he argued that the ripple effects of drug Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/
2 addiction extended beyond the immediate users, impacting family dynamics, educational outcomes,
and overall community well- being.

sentences.text: 9. Learned Special Government Pleader further argued that the prolonged nature of Court proceedings could potentially allow detenu to continue harming society while out on bail and also poses risk at large in the view of repeated offences.
It was also argued that this preventive detention is not merely punitive, but serves a crucial preventive function aimed at breaking the cycle of drug peddling and its associated crime.

Thus, removing detenu from society, ensuring a balance between public safety and individual rights demonstrate a comprehensive approach to combat drug related crimes while maintain due process of law.

10. Having heard the contentions put forth on either side and on perusal of records, it would be relevant at this juncture to refer to a recent decision of this Court itself in Writ Petition No.12085 of 2024 decided on 09.07.2024 wherein this Court dealing with similar situation had referred to a catena of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court i.e. in Mallada K Sri Ram vs. The State of Telangana and Ors. 1, NenavathBujji Etc. vs. The State of Telangana and Ors. 2, Shaik Nazeen vs.
State of Telangana 3, Ram Manohar Lohia vs. State of Bihar 4, KanuBiswas vs. State of West Bengal 5, Khaja Bilal Ahmed vs. State of Telangana 6and Ameena Begum vs. The State of Telangana 7 and had held as under, viz., "Under the given legal dictum in a series of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court referred to in the preceding paragraphs, we have no hesitation in reaching to the conclusion that in the instant case also only because the detenu has been charged with similar type of offences in an around sixteen cases in a span of around three years by itself cannot be said to be actions which can be brought under the purview of the detention "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order".

All these specific cases for which he has been charged are cases which are otherwise subjected to trial for the offences punishable under the provisions of Indian Penal Code and cannot be generalized and brought within the purview of public order."
11.

Keeping in view the aforesaid statutory provisions, particularly the Act of 1986 and the details which are reproduced in the preceding paragraphs, we may now refer to a recent decision of the Hon'ble (2023) 13 SCC 537 2024 SCC Online SC 367 (2023) 9 SCC 633 1965 SCC Online SC 9 (1972)
3 SCC 831 (2020) 13 SCC 632 (2023) 9 SCC 587 Supreme Court in the case of Nenavath Bujji 8 (supra).
In the said judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in paragraph Nos.23, 24 and 25 dealing with the explanation attached to Section 2(a) has held as under, viz., "23.

The explanation attached to Section 2(a) of the Act 1986 reproduced above contemplates that 'public order' shall be deemed to have been affected adversely or shall be deemed likely to be affected adversely, inter alia if any of the activities of any person referred to in Section 2(a) directly or indirectly, are causing or is likely to cause any harm, danger or alarm or feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave or widespread danger to life, property or public health.

The Explanation to Section 2(a) also provides that for the purpose of Section 2, a person shall be deemed to be "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order" when such person is a "GOONDA"
and engaged in activities which affect adversely or are likely to affect adversely the maintenance of public order.

It, therefore, becomes necessary to determine whether besides the person being a "GOONDA" his alleged activities are such which adversely affected the public order or are likely to affect the maintenance of public order.

sentences.text: The essential concept of preventive detention is that the detention of a person is not to punish him for something he has done but to prevent him from doing it.

The basis of detention is the satisfaction of the executive about the likelihood of the detenu acting in a manner,similar to his past acts, which is likely to affect adversely the maintenance of public order and, thereby prevent him, by an order of detention, from doing the 2024 SCC Online SC 367 same.
A criminal conviction on the other hand is for an act already done which can only be possible by a trial and legal evidence.
There is no parallel between the prosecution in a Court of law and a detention order under the Act 1986.
One is a punitive action and the other is a preventive act.

In one case a person is punished on proof of his guilt, and the standard is proof beyond the reasonable doubt, whereas in the other a person is detained with a view to prevent him from doing such act(s) as may be specified in the Act authorizing preventive detention.
25.
The power of preventive detention is qualitatively different from punitive detention.
The power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation.
It may or may not relate to an offence.
It is not a parallel proceeding.
It does not overlap with prosecution even if it relies on certain facts for which prosecution may be launched or may have been launched.
An order of preventive detention, may be made before or during prosecution.
An order of preventive detention may be made with or without prosecution and in anticipation or after discharge or even acquittal.
The pendency of prosecution is no bar to an order of preventive detention.
An order of preventive detention is also not a bar to prosecution.

(See :HaradhanSaha v. The State of W.B., 1974 Cri LJ 1479]"
12.

entities.text: HaradhanSaha v. The State of W.B., 1974 Cri LJ 1479
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Again in paragraph No.32, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has in great detail dealt with the expression 'law and order' and 'public order' and held as under, viz., "32.
The crucial issue is whether the activities of the detenu were prejudicial to public order.

While the expression 'law and order' is wider in scope inasmuch as contravention of law always affects order, 'Public order' has a narrower ambit, and could be affected by only such contravention, which affects the community or the public at large.
Public order is the even tempo of life of the community taking the country as a whole or even a specified locality.
The distinction between the areas of 'law and order' and 'public order' is one of degree and extent of the reach, of the act in question on society.
It is the potentiality of the act to disturb the even tempo of life of the community which makes it prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order.
If a contravention in its effect is confined only to a few individuals directly involved as distinct from a wide spectrum of public, it could raise problem of law and order only.
In other words, the true distinction between the areas of law and order and public order lies not merely in the nature or quality of the act, but in the degree and extent of its reach upon society.
Acts similar in nature, but committed in different contexts and circumstances, might cause different reactions.

In one case it might affect specific individuals only, and therefore touches the problem of law and order only,
while in another it might affect public order.
The act by itself, therefore, is not determinant of its own gravity.

In its quality it may not differ from other similar acts,
but in its potentiality, that is, in its impact on society, it may be very different.

[See:
Union of India v. Amrit Lal Manchanda, (2004) 3 SCC 75.]"

In yet another land mark decision in Ameena Begum vs. The State of Telangana 9, a judgment which has been pronounced under the same provision of law, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held at paragraph Nos.34 to 37 as under:
(2023) 9 SCC 587 "34.

entities.text: Ameena Begum vs. The State of Telangana 9
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In Kuso Sah vs. The State of Bihar, Hon'ble Y.V. Chandrachud,
J. (as the Chief Justice then was) speaking for the Bench held that:
"4.*** The two concepts have well defined contours, it being well established that stray and un-organised crimes of theft and assault are not matters of public order since they do not tend to affect the even flow of public life.

entities.text: Kuso Sah vs. The State of Bihar
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Infractions of law are bound in some measure to lead to disorder but every infraction of law does not necessarily result in public disorder.

** *
6. *** The power to detain a person without the safeguard of a court trial is too drastic to permit a lenient construction and therefore Courts must be astute to ensure that the detaining authority does not transgress the limitations subject to which alone the power can be exercised.

** *" 
(underlining ours, for emphasis)

35. Turning our attention to section 3(1) of the Act, the Government has to arrive at a subjective satisfaction that a goonda (as in the present case) has to be detained, in order to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
Therefore, we first direct ourselves to the examination of what constitutes 'public order'.
Even within the provisions of the Act, the term "public order" has, strictosensu, been defined in narrow and restricted terms.
An order of detention under section 3(1) of the Act can only be issued against a detenu to prevent him "from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order".

"Public order" is defined in the Explanation to section 2(a) of the Act as encompassing situations that cause "harm, danger or alarm or a feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave wide-spread danger to life or public health".

36. Ram Manohar Lohia (supra) is an authority to rely upon for the proposition that if liberty of an individual can be invaded under statutory rules by the simple process of making of a certain order,
he can be so deprived only if the order is in consonance with the said rule.

Strict compliance with the letter of the rule, in such a case, has to be the essence of the matter since the statute has the potentiality to interfere with the personal liberty of an individual and a Court is precluded from going behind its face.
Though circumstances may make it necessary for ordering a detention without trial, but it would be perfectly legitimate to require strict observance of the rules in such cases.
If there is any doubt whether the rules have been strictly observed, that doubt must be resolved in favour of the detenu.
37. Rekha too (supra) provides a useful guide.

It is said in paragraph 30 that:

5 "30.

sentences.text: Whenever an order under a preventive detention law is challenged one of the questions the court must ask in deciding its legality is: was the ordinary law of the land sufficient to deal with the situation?
If the answer is in the affirmative, the detention order will be illegal.
In the present case, the charge against the detenu was of selling expired drugs after changing their labels.
Surely the relevant provisions in the Penal Code and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act were sufficient to deal with this situation.
Hence, in our opinion, for this reason also the detention order in question was illegal."

14. This Bench observed that there is an adequate distinction between acts affecting public order and those merely related to law and order, where this distinction was emphasized by the Apex Court in Nenavath Bujji (supra).
This detention order does not conclusively demonstrate how the detenu's drug related activities had widespread impact on society rather than being confined to specific individuals or instances.
This lack of clear differentiation is further compounded by insufficient evidence of an imminent threat to public order, as required by the explanation in Section 2(a) of the Act.

Further, we have examined that the detention order heavily relied on the detenu's past criminal record without establishing how his release on bail would lead to an immediate disruption of public order.

Moreover, the use of preventive detention appears to be a means to circumvent the regular criminal justice process which goes against the principle that such detention should not be used as a punitive measure or as a shortcut to avoid the complexities of criminal prosecution.
15. Despite the directives from the Hon'ble Supreme Court and this Court, it is unfortunate that preventive detention continues to be routinely employed by authorities in Telangana.
As previously mentioned, preventive detention should only be applied in exceptional circumstances, specifically when an individual's actions pose a threat to public order.
The Court has repeatedly noted that authorities often struggle to differentiate between actions that disrupt law and order and those that genuinely threaten public order.

As elucidated in the Supreme Court judgments of Nenavath Bujji (supra) and Ameena Begum (supra) public order refers to the "even tempo of life of the community"
and has significantly narrower ambit than 'law and order'.
16.
In the present case, the detenu's alleged drug peddling activities though where undoubtedly serious and repetitive, but do not meet the high threshold required to justify preventive detention order.
This distinction is crucial in maintaining the delicate balance between societal protection and individual rights that forms the bedrock of our democratic legal system.

This Court further recognizes that the authorities have concerns about the detenu's repeated offenses but failed to emphasize that the frequency of alleged crimes does not automatically elevate the matter from a law and order issue to one of public order.
Furthermore, it is essential to consider that the purpose of preventive detention is not to punish past actions, but to prevent future harm to public order.
In the present case, the anticipation of potential future crimes based on past behavior does not meet the stringent criteria for preventive detention as outlined in these precedents.
17. This Bench take note that detenu has been granted bail in all pending cases with none having reached conclusion in trail, is a paramount importance in this case.

This scenario was resonate with the Rekha case, which unequivocally stated that if the ordinary law of the land is sufficient to deal Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/
6

The multiple FIRs against the detenu under NDPS Act and his subsequent bail granted demonstrates that the regular criminal justice system is not only capable but actively engaged in addressing his alleged crimes.
This engagement of the standard legal process undermines the necessity for the extraordinary measure of preventive detention.

Further, this Bench noted that the granting of bail in detenu's case suggest that the Court concerned found no immediate threat to public order or reason to believe that the detenu would evade justice if released.

The authority concerned must also consider that preventive detention laws are not meant to circumvent the regular criminal justice process or to be used as a tool for easier conviction and their application must be reserved for the most exceptional circumstances where there is clear and present danger to public order that cannot be addressed through standard legal channels.
18.

For all the aforesaid reasons and the judicial precedents referred to in the preceding paragraphs,
we are of the considered opinion that the reasoning given by respondent No.2 while passing the impugned order of preventive detention and which was affirmed by the Advisory Board is not justifiable or satisfactory becoming difficult to uphold the same.
As a consequence, the impugned order dated 03.01.2022 is liable to be and is accordingly set-aside / quashed.
The detenu, as a consequence, if he is otherwise not wanted in any other case, can be released from detention forthwith.
19. Accordingly, the Writ Petition stands allowed.
No costs.
20. As a sequel, miscellaneous petitions pending if any, shall stand closed.
